newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban planes fly sorties, peace hopes dim.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban planes fly sorties, peace hopes dim.

text.p: Taleban warplanes flew sorties over the battlefield north of Kabul on Friday and artillery pounded a village held by forces of the ousted government as efforts toward a ceasefire looked less and less likely to meet success.
The two Soviet-era warplanes, earlier seen by witnesses being loaded with 100 kg (220 lb) bombs, flew north at least half a dozen times on Friday.
At the same time, artillery of the purist Islamic militia fired at the village of Kalakan where at least 14 civilians were killed by a Taleban bomber on Thursday.

Commanders loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood have been operating out of Kalakan, 25 km (15 miles) north of Kabul, as their forces tried to break through Taleban lines over the past few days.
Taleban fighters near the front line said they tried again on Thursday night, but were repulsed. There was no independent confirmation of the report.

Reuters correspondent Chris Bird reported from the northern side of the front lines that one warplane tried to bomb the town of Jabal os-Siraj, some 70 km (44 miles) north of the capital the Taleban captured a month ago.
The bomb landed in a field and no one was hurt. There were no immediate reports of the targets of the other raids.

Bird said that hundreds of troops loyal to northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum were in Jabal os-Siraj since he allied with Masood two weeks ago and sent tanks, artillery and men to the front lines.
At the same time he was conducting ceasefire talks with the Taleban brokered by Pakistan and United Nations Special Envoy Norbert Holl.
The Taleban had said until Wednesday there was no evidence Dostum's men were in action.

However, on Thursday, Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) the Uzbeks "have openly taken part in the offensives" against the Islamist Taleban.
Mutaqi was quoted as saying that those killed included a general whose documents showed he belonged to Dostum's forces, dimming already slim hopes of a ceasefire with the two sides.

Mutaqi had said on Wednesday Dostum was a man the Taleban could do business with, but that if it did become clear his men were involved in the fighting north of Kabul, he would be regarded as an enemy.

Holl had been scheduled to fly to the southern Afghan city of Kandahar on Thursday, where the Taleban have their headquarters, but there was no immediate word on whether he had achieved a breakthrough.

Mutaqi's reference to the dead Uzbek general appeared to relate to attempts by the alliance to take the De Sabz pass on the so-called new road that then rolls across the eastern side of the dusty plain to Kabul some 30 km (19 miles) away.

Military analysts in Kabul say the alliance needs to wrest the pass from Taleban control and move down the new road to cover the flank of Masood's forces battling down the main road that runs parallel near the western side of the plain.
There, the front line is about 25 km (15 miles) north of the Kabul city limits and has been static for several days and Taleban fighters said on Friday there was still no change.
They said that apart from intermittent exchanges of fire, the fronts had been fairly quiet since Thursday afternoon.

The relative lull enabled hundreds of refugees to flee the combat zone on Friday morning, most of them in dozens of trucks loaded with bundles, bedding and furniture with men, women and children riding on top.
